title: Between-bucket settlement lock-in can lock YES off the instantaneous METAR reading despite a lower authoritative daily-high, contradicting its own documented invariant
description: settlement_monitor._check_between_settlement()'s YES branch computes `comp_temp = max(current_temp_f, max_temp_f)` and locks YES when `max_temp_f is not None and lower_f <= comp_temp <= upper_f`. When the freshest instantaneous reading (current_temp_f) exceeds the independently-cached authoritative running daily high (max_temp_f), comp_temp reduces to current_temp_f and the lock is decided purely by the instantaneous reading -- contradicting the function's own docstring ('YES only from a REAL max_temp_f; never locks YES from the current_temp_fallback alone') and the test named for that exact invariant, which only covers max_temp_f=None.
root_cause: The `max(current_temp_f, max_temp_f)` combination silently substitutes the instantaneous reading for the authoritative running extreme whenever the instantaneous reading is larger, defeating the 'requires a REAL max_temp_f' guard exactly in the still-rising-temperature case the guard exists to protect against.
evidence: Reproduced this session: `_check_between_settlement(current_temp_f=67.0, lower_f=66.5, upper_f=68.5, max_temp_f=65.0)` returns `{'locked': True, 'outcome': 'yes', 'confidence': 0.7749999999999999, 'comp_temp_f': 67.0}` — comp_temp_f == current_temp_f, confirming the lock is decided by the instantaneous reading while max_temp_f (65.0) is still below the band. Verified tests/test_settlement_monitor.py's TestCheckBetweenSettlement class (L126-272) in full: every test that supplies a non-None max_temp_f sets current_temp_f == max_temp_f (never current_temp_f > max_temp_f), so the gap is untested. Verified downstream: cron.py L1434-1497 reads settlement signals and auto-closes any matching open paper trade via paper.close_paper_early() once confidence>=0.80, with no ticker-family distinction and no human review; also confirmed the between-bucket branch (settlement_monitor.py L401-453) never calls _calibrate_metar_settlement_confidence (only the T-ticker branch at L455-478 does), so its raw confidence (up to 0.95) is used directly against the 0.80 gate.
expected_behavior: YES should only lock when the authoritative running daily-high value (max_temp_f) itself is confirmed inside the band with sufficient clearance -- not whenever the momentarily-larger of {current_temp_f, max_temp_f} happens to be in-band.
actual_behavior: The function locks YES using comp_temp_f == current_temp_f whenever current_temp_f > max_temp_f, even though max_temp_f (the value the docstring says is required) is itself still below the band.
recommendation: Gate the in-band/YES check on max_temp_f itself, not max(current_temp_f, max_temp_f); use current_temp_f only for the already-correctly-reasoned NO branch. Add a regression test with max_temp_f present-but-lower-than-current_temp_f.
financial_risk: Feeds paper.close_paper_early() with no human review; a forced YES close on a temperature that has only just entered the band and may still climb books an incorrect settlement outcome, corrupting paper P&L, which per d320142d's commit message feeds paper.is_accuracy_halted()'s rolling win-rate that trading_gates.LiveTradingGate also checks -- several steps removed from live-money impact and unverified in this worktree, but a real risk-control input nonetheless.
reproduction: Reproduced this session via direct call: `_check_between_settlement(current_temp_f=67.0, lower_f=66.5, upper_f=68.5, max_temp_f=65.0)` -> confidence 0.775, comp_temp_f=67.0. Also independently recomputed the confidence formula by hand and it matches.
limitations: Whether this code path has actually executed in production (vs. just being scheduled/dormant) is unverifiable from this worktree.
verification_notes: Independently re-verified this session against current code (not trusting the original finding's own description). Read settlement_monitor.py:200-330 in full, re-ran the exact repro live and got byte-identical output to what the finding claims, and read the entire TestCheckBetweenSettlement test class in tests/test_settlement_monitor.py to independently confirm the claimed test-coverage gap (no test uses max_temp_f present-but-lower-than-current_temp_f). Also independently confirmed cron.py's downstream consumer behavior and that the between-bucket branch skips METAR calibration (grep for _calibrate_metar_settlement_confidence call sites: only L469 in the T-ticker branch). No discrepancies found; upgraded confidence to VERY HIGH given the live reproduction.

title: Kill-switch override rename race can crash cmd_cron with uncaught FileExistsError (Path.rename vs os.replace semantics gap)
description: main.py's cmd_cron() wrapper implements a one-shot interactive override for the kill switch: when an operator answers 'y' to 'Override and run this cycle anyway?', it does `_kill_path.rename(_kill_tmp)` (main.py:332) to temporarily move .kill_switch out of the way, restoring it in a `finally` block afterward. This rename is NOT wrapped in try/except. Unlike the rest of the codebase's atomic-write infrastructure (safe_io.atomic_write_json / os.replace, hardened across cluster J commits 94d36402/3a28ae33 specifically because Path.rename()/os.replace() differ on Windows), this call site uses Path.rename(), which raises FileExistsError if the destination already exists, rather than atomically replacing it the way os.replace() does. The repo's own bare-os.replace bypass guard test only regex-matches `os.replace(`, not `.rename(`, so these 3 rename call sites (all in this one function) were never brought into that migration's scope.
root_cause: A stale .kill_switch.tmp can be left on disk if the cron watchdog (cron.py:2375 os._exit, 720s timeout) hard-kills the process mid-override-cycle (os._exit bypasses Python `finally` blocks, so the restore-from-tmp step at main.py:346-350 never runs). If, in that same aborted cycle, a black-swan check re-creates .kill_switch (a scenario the finally block's own comment explicitly anticipates: 'black swan re-created it during the run'), the next manual cmd_cron invocation's stale-tmp-restore guard (main.py:290: `_kill_stale_tmp.exists() and not _kill_path.exists()`) is False -- because .kill_switch now exists again -- so the orphaned .kill_switch.tmp is never cleaned up. If the operator then answers 'y' to another override prompt, main.py:332's rename target (.kill_switch.tmp) already exists, and Path.rename() raises FileExistsError uncaught.
evidence: Grepped `\.rename(` across the entire repo (excluding tests/audit) -- exactly 3 hits, all in main.py's cmd_cron wrapper (lines 292, 332, 350); only line 332 is unguarded by try/except or a pre-check that the destination is absent. Directly reproduced in this Windows environment this session: `pathlib.Path('a').rename(pathlib.Path('b'))` where b already exists raises `FileExistsError [WinError 183] Cannot create a file when that file already exists`. Independently confirmed cron.py:2375 `os._exit(1)` is a real watchdog armed inside cron.cmd_cron (reached from main.py's override branch at L342), with its own comment 'hard kill -- no cleanup; preferred over sys.exit so finally blocks don't re-hang'. Independently confirmed the 'black swan re-created it' scenario is a real code path, not speculative: alerts.py:564 activate_black_swan_halt() calls _KILL_SWITCH_PATH.touch() (L582), and cron.py:1034 runs run_black_swan_check unconditionally every cycle including during a user override (per the surrounding comment).
expected_behavior: The kill-switch override mechanism should never crash with an uncaught exception regardless of what state a prior hard-killed override run left the .kill_switch/.kill_switch.tmp files in; it should either restore/replace atomically (os.replace semantics) or detect and clean up an orphaned .tmp file before attempting another rename.
actual_behavior: Under the compound race described (hard-kill by watchdog + black-swan re-creation during the same aborted override cycle, followed by a second manual override attempt), main.py:332 raises an uncaught FileExistsError, crashing the CLI invocation instead of running the override cycle or failing gracefully.
recommendation: Use os.replace() (or safe_io's retry-wrapped equivalent) instead of Path.rename() at main.py:332/292/350 so the operation is atomic-replace rather than fail-on-exists; additionally, change the stale-tmp-restore guard at main.py:290 to also unlink an orphaned .kill_switch.tmp when .kill_switch already exists (mirroring the finally block's own `if _kill_tmp.exists(): if _kill_path.exists(): _kill_tmp.unlink()` logic), rather than only handling the not-exists case.
financial_risk: Low/none directly -- the kill switch remains present/active throughout this failure (fail-safe direction: trading stays halted), and the crash only occurs on a manual interactive `py main.py cron` invocation (the automated loop path skips this whole block via `_called_from_loop`). title: execution_log.py and tracker.py never explicitly close SQLite connections
description: _conn() in both files returns a raw sqlite3.connect(...) object used via `with _conn() as con:`. sqlite3.Connection's context-manager protocol only commits/rolls back the transaction on exit -- it does not close the connection. Neither file ever calls con.close().

evidence: Independently re-ran the grep: execution_log.py has exactly 21 `with _conn() as con:` blocks and 0 `con.close()` calls; tracker.py has exactly 105 and 0 respectively -- both counts match the finding's own citation exactly. expected_behavior: Ideally each connection is explicitly closed after use, or a longer-lived pooled connection is used deliberately.
actual_behavior: In CPython, the connection is typically closed promptly via refcounting once the local variable goes out of scope, so this has low practical impact under normal execution, but is not guaranteed by the `with` idiom itself.
recommendation: No urgent action needed given CPython's refcounting behavior; consider explicit con.close() in a finally block if this code is ever run under an alternate Python implementation or under heavy concurrent connection churn.
financial_risk: None observed.
reproduction: Not reproduced; verified via independent grep and standard sqlite3 module semantics.
limitations: Long-standing, low-severity pattern; not connected to the recent commit window specifically.
verification_notes: Fully confirmed; independent grep counts (21/0 in execution_log.py, 105/0 in tracker.py) matched the finding's implicit counts exactly, and the sqlite3.Connection.__exit__ semantics claim is correct, standard, documented Python behavior.
priority: P3 - low, mitigated by CPython refcounting in practice

title: cron._acquire_cron_lock() has a TOCTOU race with no OS-level exclusive-create primitive — reproduced
description: _acquire_cron_lock() checks `if lp.exists(): ...` and, several lines later, calls `lp.write_text(json.dumps(lock_data))` with no intervening OS-level exclusive-create (no O_EXCL open, no msvcrt.locking, no atomic rename-based claim). Two processes racing to acquire the lock when it does not yet exist (or has just gone stale) can both observe exists()==False and both proceed to write, each believing it holds exclusive ownership. This is the ONLY mechanism serializing cmd_cron (cron.py:2409) against cmd_watch --auto's own trade cycle (main.py:3622), web_app.py's /api/run_cron spawn path, and the emos-train/emos-deactivate 'cron in flight' pre-checks (main.py:6682, 6820).

evidence: Self-reproduced this session by running audit/reproductions/cron_lock_race_repro.py (redirects cron.LOCK_PATH to a tempdir, monkeypatches pathlib.Path.exists to rendezvous two threads at a threading.Barrier the instant both have evaluated `if lp.exists():`, then releases both into the write path). Output: `results: [True, True]` — both callers of _acquire_cron_lock() returned True, i.e. both believe they hold the exclusive lock.
expected_behavior: At most one caller should ever be able to acquire the cron lock at a given moment; a second concurrent acquisition attempt should observe the first caller's lock and return False.
actual_behavior: Both racing callers can return True and proceed to run a full trading cycle concurrently.
recommendation: Replace the exists()-then-write_text() pattern with an atomic exclusive-create, e.g. `open(lp, 'x')` (raises FileExistsError if the file already exists) wrapped in the same fail-closed exception handling already present, or reuse paper.py's msvcrt-based _CrossProcessDataLock primitive for this file too.
financial_risk: If two lock holders both run a trade cycle concurrently, each can independently detect the same open live position needing a protective exit (verified cron.py:912-919 calls _check_live_position_exits/_check_live_model_exits on live positions left open from a prior watch --auto --live session) and each submit its own real IOC sell order to Kalshi. execution_log.record_live_exit_fill's compare-and-set (execution_log.py:648-681,734+) prevents double-counting the P&L row but cannot prevent the second real order from reaching the exchange, since that gate only runs after both orders have already been placed. Also amplifies execution_log.was_recently_ordered/was_traded_today (execution_log.py:278-325), which are plain SELECT-then-later-INSERT checks with no DB UNIQUE constraint and rely entirely on this lock's (currently broken) single-holder guarantee.
security_risk: None (not attacker-reachable — requires two legitimate local invocations racing).
reproduction: python audit/reproductions/cron_lock_race_repro.py — deterministic via a threading.Barrier rendezvous inside a monkeypatched Path.exists; no repo data touched (LOCK_PATH redirected to a tempdir).
limitations: Reproduced via two threads within one process racing on Path.exists/write_text, which validates the code-level TOCTOU logic; a fully faithful two-OS-process reproduction was not attempted this session (not necessary to establish the flaw, since the race window is in the shared function's own logic regardless of thread vs. process boundary).

title: trade_cycle.py's prewarm ThreadPoolExecutor tasks are not cancelled on timeout and outlive the phase that spawned them

title: ForecastCache disk snapshot is last-writer-wins across independent processes
description: ForecastCache/PersistentForecastCache's store is strictly in-process (self._store: dict), so separate cron/watch/web_app processes each hold an independent copy; dump_to_disk/load_from_disk round-trip through a single shared JSON file with no cross-process merge — the last process to dump_to_disk() wins and silently discards any newly-learned entries a losing process added.
root_cause: dump_to_disk builds its serialized payload purely from the calling instance's own in-memory self._store and does a full atomic_write_json overwrite; load_from_disk likewise fully replaces in-memory entries from whatever the file currently contains — no read-merge-write.
evidence: Read forecast_cache.py:185-227 directly, confirming the full-overwrite/full-replace shape with no merge step.
expected_behavior: N/A for this severity — flagged for completeness per the pass's shared-mutable-state scope, not because a merge is necessarily warranted.
actual_behavior: A newly-learned cache entry (e.g. a station lookup) in one process can be silently discarded if another process dumps its own (older) snapshot afterward.
recommendation: No action needed given the low-impact caches involved; if this pattern is reused for higher-value state in the future, a read-merge-write should be considered.
financial_risk: None — the caches affected are documented as permanent/idempotent derived facts (e.g. station lookups) that get re-derived next time needed, not trading state.
reproduction: Not reproduced; assessed via direct code reading.
limitations: E1 only.
verification_notes: Read forecast_cache.py:185-227 directly. dump_to_disk (L185-203) confirmed exactly as described: builds `serializable` purely from self._store, single atomic_write_json call, full overwrite — this is the actual mechanism causing last-writer-wins loss and is fully confirmed. MINOR CORRECTION to the finding's description of load_from_disk (L206-227): it does NOT 'fully replace' in-memory entries — the loop does `self._store[str_to_key(k_str)] = (value, now)` per key with no preceding self._store.clear(), so it is a per-key MERGE of disk entries into whatever is already in memory (disk wins on key conflicts, but non-conflicting in-memory-only entries survive a load). title: graduation_check()'s Brier-score VALUE (the 0.23 threshold gating ALL live trading) has zero ticker-family/condition_type filtering — rain/hurricane/storm-order shadow-market predictions contaminate the temperature-trading calibration score that authorizes real money
priority: P0
description: trading_gates.LiveTradingGate.check()'s final and most decisive sub-check is paper.graduation_check(), which requires tracker.brier_score(last_n=50) <= 0.23. brier_score() pools ALL settled multiday predictions regardless of condition_type/ticker family (temperature, monthly rain, monthly snow, hurricane-count, hurricane-next-event, storm-order), while its sibling count_settled_predictions() (used for the paired sample-size gate) was already fixed on 2026-07-30 to exclude exactly these non-temperature condition types. brier_score() never received the equivalent fix, so the value compared against the 0.23 threshold and the sample-size gate it's paired with now draw from two inconsistent, partially-overlapping populations, and the score itself remains contaminated by market types that have nothing to do with whether the actual temperature-trading strategy (the only one that receives real capital) is well-calibrated.
root_cause: tracker.brier_score()'s SQL query has no WHERE clause filtering on condition_type/ticker family, unlike its sibling count_settled_predictions() which was patched on 2026-07-30 (per its own docstring referencing a prior backlog fix) to exclude 'between', 'precip_month_total', 'snow_month_total', 'hurricane_count', 'hurricane_next_event', 'storm_order'. Since 2026-08-06/08-07, order_executor._auto_place_trades routes several shadow-only, immature, statistically unrelated market families through _log_shadow_predictions()/tracker.log_prediction(is_shadow=True), and that shadow-logging rationale (originally intended for temperature-market signals shadow-logged during a pause/cap) was never revisited once expanded to cover entirely different market types.
evidence: Independently re-read tracker.py:1917-1972 (brier_score) confirming zero condition_type/ticker-family filtering anywhere in the SQL. Independently re-read count_settled_predictions() (tracker.py:2161-2232) confirming its WHERE clause explicitly excludes 'between','precip_month_total','snow_month_total','hurricane_count','hurricane_next_event','storm_order'. Reviewer queried the real production predictions.db (read-only, via paths.py's main-clone resolution) this session, reproduced graduation_check()'s exact query logic (multiday_predictions/outcomes_valid join, ORDER BY settled_at DESC LIMIT 50), and computed the Brier score two ways on the identical window: as currently coded (all 50 rows, contaminated) = 0.2169; temperature-only (33 of the 50 rows) = 0.2381. The temperature-only score exceeds the 0.23 threshold while the contaminated score does not.
expected_behavior: The Brier score compared against graduation_check()'s 0.23 threshold should reflect only the temperature-trading strategy that actually receives live capital, consistent with the sample-size gate (count_settled_predictions) it is paired with.
actual_behavior: brier_score(last_n=50) pools temperature, rain, hurricane, and storm-order shadow predictions together. Reproduced against the real production predictions.db this session: of the most recent 50 settled rows, 17/50 (34%) are non-temperature-market rows. The contaminated score as currently computed (0.2169) sits below the 0.23 gate (passes), while the temperature-only score computed on the same window (0.2381) would fail the gate — a threshold-flipping discrepancy demonstrated on real, current production data.
recommendation: Add the same condition_type exclusion list count_settled_predictions() already uses to brier_score()'s WHERE clause, so the value compared against the 0.23 graduation threshold reflects only the temperature-trading strategy that actually receives live capital.
financial_risk: This is the terminal, most-decisive check in trading_gates.LiveTradingGate.check() — the single authorization gate for every live order in the system. A contaminated Brier score can silently authorize live trading when the temperature strategy's own calibration is too poor to trade, or conversely block a genuinely well-calibrated strategy. Currently dormant in this worktree (LIVE_TRADING_ENABLED unset), but this is a structural defect in the master go/no-go authorization for real capital, independently reproduced against real production data.
